title: Source-owned session immutability
summary: The session validates each event, takes a detached JSON copy and deep-freezes it before it enters the log, so no caller can later rewrite stored history. The protection is always on and lives in the session, not in an optional development plugin.
firstReason: The goal (history that no holder of a reference can rewrite) stands, but JavaScript's Object.freeze has no Go equivalent; the Go session should own an encoded or copied record and hand out copies or read-only views instead.

title: Event-sourced sessions with derived message history
summary: A session is an append-only log of typed events and is the single source of truth; the message history sent to the model is derived from it, and replay or fork means seeding a new session with an existing log. Appends never wait for disk; persistence buffers writes and drains them at a flush checkpoint at each turn end.
firstReason: Event sourcing does not depend on the language and is what makes replay, fork and request reconstruction possible, so the Go design should keep it.

title: Session surface — an ordered projection over the event log
summary: The ordered list of events that produce model messages (the surface) is derived and cached, and is maintained by markers in the log. Two operations, append and replace-range, let plugins such as compaction rewrite history durably and record which events each replacement used.
firstReason: Surface operations are what make compaction and other history edits replayable and checkable; nothing about them depends on JavaScript.

title: Retain ignorable session events for external plugins
summary: The session event envelope keeps its optional ignorable marker, and one helper writes ignorable plugin records in a plugin namespace, because a third-party plugin depends on readers accepting its informational events.
firstReason: Plugin processes in the Go design will write their own events, and a host without that plugin must still be able to read the session, so the marker and the plugin namespace are needed.

title: Embed Assistant streams in v2 attempt settlements
summary: The session log has no per-token chunk events. Each model attempt is stored as one record that embeds its compact timed stream: assistant/message for a visible response, assistant/attempt for a failed or retried one.
firstReason: One record per attempt keeps exact stream replay while cutting the event count; the Go format should start in this shape.

title: The system prompt is surface node 0
summary: The system prompt is an ordinary surface event, system/message, placed first; changing the prompt uses the same append and replace operations as any other message.
firstReason: Treating the prompt like every other model-visible message removes a special case from request reconstruction; keep it.

title: Canonical V3 Session event envelopes
summary: Session events use one canonical envelope: every model-visible event must carry its surface operation, log-only events may carry only type, sequence, time, data and the ignorable marker, and each fact has exactly one spelling.
firstReason: A strict canonical envelope prevents two readers from disagreeing about the same record; the Go format should adopt the same strictness from its first version.

title: Deprecate synchronous reads of arbitrary Session events
summary: Reading arbitrary old events from a session synchronously is deprecated, because the full log will not always be held in memory; state needed after resume must come from durable event fields and projections.
firstReason: The Go session interface should simply not offer synchronous random access to history; the direction is adopted, and the lint rule and deprecation markers are then unnecessary.

title: Plugin-owned message projections
summary: A plugin that owns an event which changes derived message content supplies a pure projection function for it; the session applies it atomically and refuses a log whose required projection is missing.
firstReason: This keeps feature-specific message transformations out of the session core while keeping derivation deterministic; keep it.

title: First-class tool-role messages
summary: A tool result is stored as its own tool-role message, matching what model providers expect, instead of a block inside a user message.
firstReason: The Go format should store tool results as tool-role messages from its first version; the V3 to V4 conversion is not needed.

title: Logical session and storage rebuild
summary: Proposal (not built upstream): consumers depend on a logical session interface and a session service that creates, opens, forks and flushes sessions; a private storage provider interface owns durable data, migration, repair and the writer lease.
firstReason: Adopt as the starting shape. A new Go design can define the session interface, the service and the storage provider separately from day one, without upstream's staged migration.

title: Session capability protocols
summary: Proposal (not built upstream): the session system is a small logical core plus separate capabilities (storage, projection, query); product code knows only the logical session and the session service, and only composition and providers know physical implementations.
firstReason: Adopt. It states the target boundaries of the same refactor and fits Go interfaces directly.

title: Runtime schemas for the event vocabulary (Zod vs the merge-extensible-map pattern)
summary: Rejected upstream: replacing the compile-time extensible type maps for events and content blocks with a runtime schema registry was declined as a repository-wide redesign with too little benefit.
firstReason: The rejection does not hold in Go. Go has no declaration merging, so components and plugin processes can only extend the event vocabulary through a runtime registry that maps each event type to a Go type and a validator.

title: Developer messages for incremental session changes
summary: A change to the set of tools the model can see is recorded in the session as a structured `developer/message` event, in conversation order. An addition stores only the tool name and points at the earlier request header that holds its schema.
firstReason: Providers can only keep the cached conversation prefix if tool changes are replayed exactly, including after restart and fork; free-form reminder text would lose the tool identity. The Go event format may differ (DH-ADR-2) but the record and its strict reference checks are needed.

title: Recorded user-source attribution compatibility
summary: A producer may add a new 'attribution-only' kind to the source field of persisted user messages without a session format version bump, under a recorded compatibility policy checked against schema fingerprints. Prompts that are only sent to the model and never stored use a separate input type with no id or source.
firstReason: The goal stands: adding an attribution label must not break older readers, and request-only prompts must not pose as session messages. The mechanism is tied to upstream's TypeScript union fingerprints and its released formats; the Go design states its own forward-compatibility rule (readers keep unknown source kinds) in its event schema.

title: Active tool headers and stateful request projection
summary: Each model request header records the assembled active tools. The loop compares names with the previous header and logs one developer message with additions and removals; the session caches a fold of this tool history that requests and compaction reuse.
firstReason: Plugin and MCP tools change mid-conversation, and providers differ in how they accept that. A capability-independent history lets each provider adapter project it its own way without re-declaring or dropping tools. It is needed in Go because plugin processes come and go the same way.

title: Ordinary forks have no durable creator relationship
summary: An ordinary fork copies history but records no link to its source session. Only subagents record their creator, and `origin: subagent` classifies them.
firstReason: Using one parent field for both copied history and delegation made forks look like subagents, with false child notifications and hidden sessions. The Go session header should have separate fields from the start.

title: Remove synthetic turns for log-only events
summary: A plugin that records a log-only event while no turn is running appends it directly to the session and, if it promised durability, flushes explicitly. No artificial turn is opened just to get a durability checkpoint.
firstReason: A turn identifier should mean one model-loop execution and nothing else. The Go session log can allow extension events between turns in the same way.

title: Drop durable step boundary events
summary: Rejected proposal: remove the `step/start` and `step/end` events from the session log. Upstream keeps them, because `step/end` is the durable sign that a model request finished, and the pair makes crash repair, invariants and reading a transcript clearer.
firstReason: The rejection still holds in Go. Knowing that a step finished without inferring it from neighbouring events is a property of the log, not of the language, and crash repair depends on it.
